description: Fullstack разработчик, интересуюсь космическими технологиями, ищу людей которые могут создать софт и грамотно его отполировать
summary: Astronaut Health Monitor is a Mission Control style dashboard that lets a four-person crew see, forecast and act on the state of their health when the ground is far away: at Mars, a question to a flight surgeon and its answer take 6 to 45 minutes. It tracks every indicator the challenge names (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep and mood) plus SpO2, respiration, ECG, cabin air and radiation. It combines real physiological recordings (PhysioNet), real solar flares (NASA DONKI), live space weather (NOAA GOES) and cabin and radiation limits taken from NASA-STD-3001 and related NASA documents, and every number says whether it is recorded, modelled or an engineering choice. A Time-to-Threshold forecast warns before a limit is crossed, a prioritised alarm gives the first action to take, and the advice on contacting the ground adapts to where the crew is (station, Moon or Mars). Every indicator explains itself in plain language and is linked to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, and the app keeps working with an in-browser simulation when the connection is lost.
details:
Live app: https://astronaut-health-monitor-one.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/Akhmadov-360/nasa-hackaton-2026 · Slides: https://astronaut-health-monitor-one.vercel.app/deck · PDF-file: https://astronaut-health-monitor-one.vercel.app/deck/deck.pdf

The problem

On long missions the crew must spot health changes in themselves, and ground support is delayed: about 1.3 s to the Moon, roughly 3 to 22 minutes one way to Mars. A health tool for that crew must explain its readings, warn early, say what to do first, and keep working without a link to Earth.

What it does

  • One screen for a crew of four: an anatomical body scan with clickable organs, a recorded ECG, vitals (heart rate, SpO2, blood pressure, respiration, HRV, stress, temperature), cabin metrics (O2, CO2, humidity, noise, airflow) and radiation (a modelled crew dose plus live GOES proton flux). Status is always an icon, a word and a colour, never colour alone.
  • Forecast before the limit: a Time-to-Threshold forecast in the status island and on each card. It fires only on a steady trend (R² ≥ 0.8, at most 3 minutes ahead), so a step or noise never forecasts.
  • Act first: a prioritised flight log with pinned alarms, voice alerts, a short "Do now" first action for any out-of-range reading, and a Ground line that depends on where the crew is (station, Gateway, Moon base, Mars transit, Mars base).
  • The astronaut is a sensor too: a self-check of blood glucose, sleep, mood and water, with routine check-in reminders by mission-day hour and a day streak. Entries are judged against the same limits and flow into the log, report and exports.
  • Explains itself: an About window for every indicator (why it matters, what spaceflight does to it, how it is measured, how to keep it healthy, when to seek help), a trend chart with limit bands, and its link to NASA's five hazards and named HRP risks.
  • Report and replay: a medical report with a limits-and-sources table, Time Travel replay of any moment, and export to Excel, CSV and a validated telemetry package.

How it works

  • A deterministic engine, frame(t) = baseline(t) + modifiers(t), runs identically on the server and in the browser. Each visitor gets their own simulation, and source modes LIVE → POLL → STALE → SIM keep monitoring going when the network drops.
  • Every limit carries a tier (nasa, derived, clinical, engineering, provisional) and a source, so the crew can see what to trust. Scenario responses are modelled and labelled as such.
  • Stack: Next.js, React and TypeScript (web), NestJS with WebSocket (API), Zod-validated contracts, GSAP and Three.js for the pitch slides. Unit tests cover the engine, data, API and web app, and an 18-step browser test runs the whole story end to end. Interface in English, Russian and an Uzbek draft.

Benefits and intended impact

Built for Mars, useful wherever the doctor is far away: polar and research stations, ships, and remote districts on Earth where help is hours away. The same flow applies: forecast, first action, report sent when the link allows.

Honest limits

A prototype, not a medical device; the crew is fictional. Guidance is illustrative and not validated by flight surgeons. Not built yet: bone and muscle models, camera input, symptom entry, a reviewed Uzbek translation.
